chunks: "The inductor has two very different ends.
One end is the switch node, which swings the full input voltage in nanoseconds, so I put the inductor right next to the SW pins and keep that copper short and small.
The other end is the output node, carrying smooth ripple current, so I take it to the output capacitors with wide, short copper, because there the concern is resistance, not inductance.
The inductor body is also a magnetic field source.

I keep the feedback trace, the divider and any sensitive analog circuitry away from it, and I orient it so its field isn't pointing at them; with several inductors I rotate them 90 degrees apart and space them.
A shielded inductor helps a lot when space is tight.
I don't route signals under an unshielded inductor, and I check the datasheet about copper pours or planes underneath, since some vendors recommend a keep-out for the best inductance.
Last, heat: the winding dissipates I squared DCR, so I give its pads copper, and I keep temperature-sensitive parts away. For the numbers: with 12 volts in, 3. 3 volts out and 4.
7 microhenries, the ripple slope is about 1. 85 amps per microsecond, so a 10 nanohenries mutual coupling into a feedback loop gives about 18 millivolts of pickup."
